findings.title: Short sleep while the lifts aren't progressing
findings.data: Sleep averaged 6h 06m over 28 nights in the last 4 weeks, under the 7 hours adults need, and your main lifts have not progressed over the last 8 weeks (Bench Press −2.7%, Squat +2.9%).
findings.evidence: In a trial, five nights of 4 hours' sleep left muscle protein synthesis about a fifth lower (Saner 2020), and a review links short sleep with lower strength in compound lifts (Knowles 2018).

findings.title: Short sleep while the lifts aren't progressing
findings.data: Sleep averaged 6h 06m over 28 nights in the last 4 weeks, under the 7 hours adults need, and your main lifts are down over the last 8 weeks (Bench Press −12.1%, Squat −7.1%).
findings.evidence: In a trial of dieting adults, 5.5 hours in bed instead of 8.5 lost about the same weight, but 55% less of it was fat and 60% more was lean mass (Nedeltcheva 2010). In another, five nights of 4 hours' sleep left muscle protein synthesis about a fifth lower (Saner 2020).

findings.title: Gaining faster than studies find useful
findings.data: The trend rose +0.70 %/wk over the last 4 weeks, on 3,372 kcal a day, 486 over the 2,886 target.
findings.evidence: A review for lifters puts a useful rate at about 0.25 to 0.5 % of body weight a week, less for the more trained, with faster gains adding more fat (Iraki 2019). In a trial with elite athletes, a larger surplus added more fat without adding more lean mass (Garthe 2013).

findings.title: Some food may be missing from the log
findings.data: Over the last 4 weeks you logged 1,731 kcal a day and the weight trend held (+0.03 %/wk), which puts what you burn at about 1,704 kcal a day. Lying still all day, your body would use about 2,005: 1,823 at rest plus about a tenth for digesting food.
findings.evidence: Burning less than that while up and about isn't possible, so some food is likely missing from the log, and the protein and calorie numbers from it read low too. Studies that measured real intake with doubly labelled water find self-reports usually fall short (Hill and Davies 2001), by half in some people (Schoeller 1995), including those who said they couldn't lose weight on little food (Lichtman 1992).
